transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, doctor, it’s... it’s a whole big situation, really. The people around me, they say I need to be here because my talking, it gets all... it gets all mixed up. Like, I’ll be trying to explain something, just trying to get a point across, you know? I’ll try to explain about the keys—the heavy ones I use for work, 'cause I clean the buildings, right, the big ring of brass keys—but then, while I'm talking about the keys, I have to tell them about the jail. Because it connects, you see? And then from the jail, I start talking about the prayer rug, the patterns on it, and then the chess pieces... the knights and the bishops and how they move. I try to lay it all out so they understand the whole picture, but they just stare at me. They stop me and tell me they cannot follow what I am saying. They say my words just tangle up and they can't understand me, even though I'm just trying to explain the whole thing to them. It just happens every time I try to talk lately.
Does this mixed-up talking happen all the time when you try to explain things, or are there times when you can explain yourself clearly?

Well, like I was just saying with the keys and the prayer rug and the chess pieces... it’s, it’s all the time now. It really is. I try, I really try to just give them the short version, but you can't just give a short version when everything is hooked together. 

Like just Tuesday, I was on the third floor at work—the floor with the big glass windows, the ones that take me half the night to wipe down properly because the chemical they give me leaves streaks if you don't use the microfiber cloth—and I went to tell the night manager about the mop bucket. The wheel on the left side is busted, it drags and leaves this awful black scuff mark on the linoleum, which just makes more work for me. So I start telling him about the wheel, but the wheel, you see, it’s a circle. It’s an unbroken loop. And I had to explain how that loop is exactly like the patterns on the prayer rug I was just telling you about, and how the knight moves in an L-shape on the board to break the circle, because he needs to know that to understand why the bucket is broken. It’s the mechanics of it, the way the universe turns the wheel. 

But he just held up his hand, right in my face, like a stop sign. He actually told me to stop talking and said he had no earthly idea what I was saying and to just go empty the trash. So no, I can't... there aren't times when I'm clear to them anymore. To me, it’s perfectly clear, I'm giving them the whole entire picture so they really get it, but to them, they say it’s just that same tangled mess every single time I open my mouth to explain the simplest little thing. It just all pours out together.
Do you ever feel like your thoughts or the things you're talking about aren't really connected to the real world?

Well, connected to the real world... I mean, what is the real world, doctor? Because what I see, what I know is happening, it is very real. It's as real as the mop bucket or the brass keys. But other people, they tell me it's not. Like... like with the building people at work. The people who work in the offices during the day, the ones who wear the suits and leave their coffee cups half-full on the desks for me to clean up. 

I know they've marked me. I know it. It started a few weeks ago, or maybe a month, time gets a little slippery. But I noticed the hallway lights on the fourth floor. They have these motion sensors, right? But they weren't just clicking on when I walked by. They were flickering in a pattern. Three fast, one slow. And then, when I'd see the daytime staff leaving as I was coming in for my shift, they would give each other these little looks. Not big looks, not pointing, but just a tiny shift of the eyes, a little nod, right as they passed me. It was a warning. They were warning each other about me, letting the whole network know I was in the building. 

I tried to show my supervisor. I took him right to the security room, where they have all the monitors lined up, the ones that show every hallway and elevator. I made him pull up the footage from the fourth floor at 6:15 PM, right when the daytime people leave. I said, "Look, look at the lights, look at how they look at each other." And he played the tape back, and he pointed at the screen, and he said, "There's nothing there, Frank. The lights are steady, and those people didn't even look at you." He showed me the camera, plain as day. He said it was all in my head. 

But... but even when he showed me that, even when I saw the tape with my own two eyes and it looked perfectly normal... I still felt it. I still felt absolutely sure that they had marked me. The tape doesn't change what I know is happening. The real world... my real world has these warnings in it, even if the camera can't catch them. So, I guess... I guess to them, it's not connected to their real world. But to me, it's the most real thing there is. I have to be so careful now when I clean the fourth floor. I have to make sure I don't look directly at the sensors.
Do you really believe that the people in the building have marked you, or is that just a feeling you have?

Well, doctor, it’s... it’s not just a passing feeling, like when you feel a chill because someone left the loading dock door open. No, it’s... I know it. I absolutely believe it, down to my very bones. I know it sounds crazy to you, and I know my supervisor—Mr. Henderson, he's been there fifteen years, always wears those short-sleeved button-downs no matter how cold it gets—I know he showed me that security tape. 

We were standing right there in the little room with all the monitors, and the room always smells like stale coffee and ozone from all the electronics, and he pointed right at the screen. He rewound it, played it, rewound it again. And I looked at it, I really did. I stared at that little glowing square, and I saw what he saw. The lights weren't flickering three fast, one slow. The people in the suits, they were just walking to the elevators, looking at their phones or whatever it is they do. 

But even seeing that... even staring right at the proof that nothing was happening... it didn't change a thing in here, in my head, in my gut. I still felt it. I still feel it right now. I am completely, one hundred percent sure they have marked me. The tape is just... it's just a tape, you know? It only catches the surface of things. It doesn't catch the truth of what's happening. The little looks, the warnings, the way the network operates... it's real. It's so real that I have to change my whole routine. I have to push my cart down the left side of the hall, keeping my head down, making sure I don't trigger whatever system they have set up. So yes, I believe it. I believe it more than I believe that the sun is going to come up tomorrow, no matter what that camera showed.
Do you think the beliefs you have about being marked are affecting your daily life in any significant way?

Well, affecting my daily life... yes, yes it is. I mean, how could it not, right? When you're carrying around this kind of knowledge, when you know you've been marked, it... it spills over into everything. 

Like my shifts at work. I've actually missed shifts lately. Mr. Henderson, my supervisor, he told me I couldn't come in on Thursday or Friday last week because I was taking too long on the fourth floor, avoiding the sensors, and I lost out on that pay. I've even lost a couple of side cleaning jobs too, the ones I do on the weekends for the small accounting offices down on Elm Street, because they said I wasn't getting the work done and they couldn't rely on me. But I was just trying to be careful! I was trying to explain to them why I had to clean the baseboards in a specific order so the network wouldn't ping, and they just fired me.

And it's not just the work, doctor. It's my whole life. I don't even go to the mosque anymore. I used to go, you know, regular as clockwork, always took my spot near the shoe racks in the back because the draft from the door keeps it cool. But I stopped going to prayers, and I stopped going to my sister's house for the Sunday family gatherings. My sister and my brother-in-law, they actually sat me down and said they just can't depend on me to show up right, or act right. They said they can't understand a single word I'm saying when I try to explain the warnings and the lights, that I just confuse everyone and upset the nieces and nephews. So I just stopped joining them. It's easier that way, just staying away from people so I don't have to see them looking at me.

But even then, even when I'm alone, sometimes it gets so heavy, this feeling that they're watching and warning each other. It gets so overwhelming that I don't even know what I'm doing, and things get bad. There was a time just recently, out by the loading dock... I got so caught up in the patterns and trying to stop them from tracking me that I guess I got really unsafe. I don't remember all of it perfectly, just the freezing cold air and my heart hammering in my chest, but I was out by the dumpsters in just my undershirt in the middle of the night. I was trying to dismantle the security floodlights with a broken mop handle, and the night guard had to call for emergency help. They actually had to call an ambulance and the police to come get me because they said I was a danger to myself, slipping on the ice and screaming at the brick wall. So yes, it... it affects everything. Everything is broken now because of it.
Do you often find yourself having trouble sticking to one topic when you're talking to someone?

Well, sticking to one topic... yes, that is... honestly, doctor, that is exactly what brings me here. My talking, it just gets all mixed up lately. I don't mean for it to happen, I really don't, but there is just so much going on up here and it all needs to come out at once so people can understand the whole picture. 

Like, I will be trying to explain something very important to someone, trying to make them see how everything fits together. I try to explain about the keys—my heavy brass work keys on that big metal ring, the ones that clink against my leg when I push the mop bucket—and how those keys are connected to the jail. Because the jail has those heavy doors, you know, just like the maintenance closets on the fourth floor, locking people in and keeping things out. But then, right in the middle of explaining the jail, I realize they need to know about the prayer rug to really get it. The green prayer rug with the gold fringe that I used to kneel on before the network started tracking me. And from the prayer rug, well, it just naturally leads me to the chess pieces. The knights and the pawns, the way they move in specific patterns across the board, jumping over things just like how I have to move down the hallways to avoid the sensors. 

To me, doctor, it is a perfectly straight line. One thing leads right into the exact next thing, clear as day. But when the words actually come out of my mouth, people just look at me like I am speaking a completely different language. They tell me they cannot follow what I am saying. My sister does it, Mr. Henderson does it... they just rub their temples or shake their heads and tell me I am jumping all over the place, going from the keys to the jail to the rug to the chess pieces. They say I am not making any sense and they just cannot keep up with my sentences. 

But I have to explain all of it! If I leave out the chess pieces, then the prayer rug doesn't make sense, and if I don't talk about the jail, you won't understand the keys. There are just so many pieces to the puzzle, and I try so hard to give them the whole picture so they can see what I see, but they just get frustrated. They tell me I am confusing them and they stop listening to me, and I am just left standing there in the hallway trying to finish the thought, trying to show them how it all connects... but the words just keep getting tangled up.
Has your way of talking and thinking always been like this, or is this something that has changed over time?

Well, no, doctor... no, it hasn't always been this way. I used to be a very quiet man, you know? I just kept my head down, pushed my broom, emptied the bins, and went home. But this... this rush in my head, the way the words all pile up and spill out tangled together... that started about two years and five months ago. Exactly two years and five months, actually. It was right after... well, right after that brief detention I had, over the misunderstanding at the building. 

You see, it was just a misunderstanding, but it changed everything. I was down near the south stairwell, just trying to arrange the wet floor signs in a specific triangle so the sensors wouldn't trip and track me, and the night security—the guys with the heavy boots and the radios on their shoulders that always hiss static—they didn't understand what I was doing. They thought I was doing something wrong, tampering with the fire doors or something. So they detained me. They called it just a brief detention, but they put me in this little concrete room down by the boiler. It was so hot in there, doctor, and it smelled like burnt dust and industrial bleach, and they just left me sitting there on this cold metal folding chair while they tried to figure it out. 

And while I was sitting there, just listening to the pipes groan and feeling the vibrations from the boiler right through the rubber soles of my work boots... that’s when my mind just... it just started racing. I realized how close I came to being locked away for good, like in a real jail, all because they didn't understand the patterns and the warnings. I realized I hadn't been explaining it right. When they finally let me go, when Mr. Henderson finally came down and cleared it all up as a misunderstanding and said I was just the janitor... my head wasn't the same. 

Ever since then, for two years and five months now, my brain has been running like a floor buffer that won't shut off. I never used to talk this much, but now I have to, because if I don't, they might misunderstand again. They might lock me in that basement room again and leave me there. So I talk, and I think, and I try to lay out all the pieces for people—the keys, the rug, the sensors—but it all gets jumbled up because there's just so much to say and so much they need to know to keep me safe. So, no, it wasn't always like this. Just since that night they detained me. That's when the tangling started, two years and five months ago, and it just hasn't stopped since.
Do you often find yourself having thoughts that are not connected to each other in a logical way?

Well, connected in a logical way... I don't know about logical, doctor, because to me, maybe there is a logic in there somewhere, but it's really about the speed. It's the sheer speed of it all that makes it so hard. My thoughts, they just run so fast. It's not just one quiet thought at a time like it used to be. It feels like... well, it feels exactly like a whole crowd of people talking inside my head all at the exact same time. Like a crowded room where everyone is shouting over each other to be heard. 

One second I'm thinking about my bills, you know, the stack of envelopes sitting on my kitchen table, worrying about the electric bill and how I lost those weekend cleaning jobs. And then, before I can even finish figuring out the math for the electricity, my brain is suddenly jumping straight to the jail. I'm right back in that concrete room thinking about being locked up, feeling the cold metal chair. And then, bam, it's not the jail anymore, it jumps right to the mosque. I'm suddenly thinking about the gold fringe on the prayer rug and the cool draft by the shoe racks in the back, wondering why I stopped going. And then, just as fast as that, my mind is completely wrapped up in cleaning chemicals. The smell of the industrial bleach, the heavy ammonia I use on the tiles, worrying if the mix is right or if it's going to leave a film on the floor that the sensors will pick up. 

It just jumps and jumps and jumps—from the bills, to the jail, to the mosque, to the cleaning chemicals—just bouncing around inside my skull. It goes so incredibly fast that before I can even catch one single thought, before I can grab hold of the worry about the bills and actually do something about it, the crowd in my head has already moved on to the bleach and the prayers. I try to reach out and stop them, to just hold onto one idea for a minute, but I can't catch a single one of them. It is so exhausting, doctor, it really is, just trying to keep up with my own brain when it is sprinting away from me like that from the moment I wake up until I finally pass out.
Do you ever hear voices or sounds that other people cannot hear?

Voices... well, I mean, I don't know about what other people hear, because I'm mostly working alone on the night shift, but... yes. Yes, doctor, I do. There is a voice. It's... it's a man's voice. 

And it always seems to happen when I'm in the mop closet—the main supply closet down by the freight elevator, the one where we keep the heavy floor buffers and the extra gallons of floor wax—or sometimes it comes right out of the air vents, those big metal grates along the baseboards in the main hallway. I'll just be standing there, you know, rinsing out the heavy cotton mop head in the utility sink, just minding my own business and trying to get the water clear, and suddenly... there he is. I hear this man, and he is saying my name. Just calling my name right out of the vent. And then he tells me... he tells me that I ruined everything. "You ruined everything." Just like that. Over and over. 

And doctor, I need you to understand, this isn't like those racing thoughts I was just telling you about. This isn't a thought inside my head. It sounds exactly as real as someone standing right beside me. I mean, it sounds as real as you sitting right there in that chair asking me the question. 

I'll drop the mop handle—it bangs against the metal bucket, makes a terrible noise echoing in that little room—and I'll spin right around, expecting to see a guy standing right over my shoulder. I've even taken my heavy work flashlight off my belt and shined it right through the slats of the air vent, thinking maybe some daytime maintenance guy got stuck in the ductwork or someone is playing a sick joke on me. But there's never anyone there. Just the dust bunnies and the hum of the HVAC unit. 

But I hear him. I hear him so clear, telling me I ruined it all, and I try to speak back to the vent, I try to tell him I didn't, I try to explain that I was just doing my job and keeping the sensors clear, but he just keeps saying it. And when I ask Mr. Henderson on patrol, when I ask if he heard the man shouting in the closet, he just shakes his head and tells me the building is empty. But I know what I heard. It's a real voice, doctor, standing right there in the room with me, even when nobody is there.
Do you feel like the voice you hear is trying to tell you something important about your situation, or is it just a noise in your head?

Important? Well... yes, doctor, it’s not just noise, it’s... it’s the whole point. It's all connected, you see. The voice is just one piece of what's happening in the building. It’s trying to tell me what I already know deep down, what I see with my own eyes every single shift. 

I actually went to my supervisor about it. I went to Mr. Henderson, and I tried to explain what was going on, and he took me back into the main security office—the one with the big bank of monitors that always smell like hot ozone and stale coffee. He sat me down in this squeaky rolling chair and he pulled up the digital footage. He rewound it, played it back, paused it, and he pointed right at the screens. He said, 'Look, there’s nothing on the camera. Nobody is messing with you, nobody is down in that hallway.' He really tried to prove it to me, going through hour by hour. 

But doctor... even when my supervisor showed me nothing was on the camera, I still knew. I still felt absolutely sure that the building people had marked me. The camera just can't see the way they do it, it's not set up to catch it. The people who work in the daytime offices, the ones with the suits and the keycard lanyards, they've marked me. And they communicate about it all the time. They use the hallway lights—they’ll have maintenance leave certain fluorescent panels dim, or they’ll flicker them in a very specific sequence right when I'm scheduled to buff that section of the floor. 

And the looks... oh, the little looks they give each other. I see it when I'm emptying the lobby bins at the end of their shift, right when they're all heading for the glass doors. They don't say a word out loud where I can hear it, but they give each other these tiny little looks, just darting their eyes toward me and then away, to warn each other about me. They are warning each other that I'm there, that I'm the one who ruined everything, exactly like the voice in the vent keeps saying. 

So Mr. Henderson can point at his blank camera screens all he wants, but the cameras don't catch the rhythm of the lights, and they don't catch those little looks they pass around. The voice isn't just noise in my head, doctor. It's the truth. It's the proof that I'm marked, and no matter how much I try to just do my job and keep the floors clean, they are all warning each other about me.
Do you have times when your thoughts are clear and organized, without all the tangling and jumping between ideas?

Clear and organized? Well, I try, doctor, I really do try to get it all lined up straight in my head before I open my mouth, but... honestly, no. Not lately. Not for a long time. In fact, that's... well, that's exactly what brings me here to see you in the first place. 

My talking, it just gets all mixed up. I'll open my mouth to explain something simple, something I really need someone to understand, but the words don't come out in a straight line at all. I'll start off trying to explain about the keys—you know, my heavy brass work keys, the master ring I clip to my belt that opens the utility closets and the freight elevator—and I'm just trying to talk about the keys, but then suddenly the words coming out of my mouth are all about the jail. I'll be talking about the cold metal chair and the concrete room, and before I can even catch my breath to correct myself, I'm already onto the prayer rug. I'm talking about the gold fringe and the mosque, and then, out of nowhere, I'm trying to explain about chess pieces. Just... chess pieces, the knights and the pawns, moving them around, and I don't even play chess, but the words just keep tumbling out of me, one right after the other, all tangled up in this big, heavy knot. 

And I look at the person I'm talking to—like my supervisor Mr. Henderson, or the people at the front desk, or the nurses here—and they just have this blank, confused look on their faces. They just stare at me, maybe tilt their heads. And they tell me... they tell me they cannot follow what I am saying. They hold up their hands and say, "Slow down, you're not making any sense, we can't follow you." 

But to me, I'm just trying to get it all out! I'm trying to explain the keys and the jail and the rug and the chess pieces, because it's all rushing at me at once and I need them to hear it. It's like I'm speaking a completely different language, doctor, and I just can't make it stop and be clear, no matter how hard I try to just say one simple, normal sentence. It just keeps spilling out all mixed up, and nobody understands a word of it, and that's why I'm sitting in this chair right now.
Do you often find it difficult to express your thoughts in a coherent and orderly manner?

Well, yes, doctor, that's... that's exactly what I was just trying to tell you a moment ago. That's the whole reason I'm sitting here in this room. It's exactly that. My talking gets all mixed up, just completely tangled together like a big ball of heavy twine that you can't find the end of. 

I try so hard to be orderly. I really do. I'll stand there, maybe holding my mop or my dustpan, and I'll try to explain something simple about the keys—my heavy work keys, you know, the ones on the big metal carabiner that I use for the basement doors, they jingle when I walk—but the words don't stay on the keys. Before I can even finish my thought, my mouth is suddenly talking about the jail. I'll be going on about the cold concrete floors and the metal bars, and then right on top of that, without even taking a single breath, I'm going on about a prayer rug. I'm describing the gold tassels and the thick woven fabric of the prayer rug, and then out of nowhere, it's chess pieces! I'm talking about moving the little wooden chess pieces around a board, the knights and the pawns, and I don't even know how to play chess, doctor! 

It just spills out of me, all these things crashing into each other, the keys and the jail and the rug and the chess pieces, one right after the other like a pile-up on the highway. And the people listening to me... they just stare. They look at me like I'm speaking a completely different language. They tell me they cannot follow what I am saying. They actually say that to my face, they hold up their hands and say, "I can't follow you, you're not making any sense." So yes, it's incredibly difficult. I try to put my thoughts in a straight line, I really try to just say the one thing I mean to say, but it all comes out sideways and backwards, and I just can't stop it from happening.
Do you feel like you're rushing to get all your thoughts out when you're talking, or is it more that you're having trouble finding the right words to express what you're thinking?

Finding the right words? No, no, doctor, it's not that I can't find the words. The words are all there, there are just... there are too many of them, and they're moving so fast. It’s definitely the rushing. My thoughts, they just run so incredibly fast, it feels exactly like there is a whole crowd of people talking inside my head all at the exact same time. Like a packed room where everybody is shouting over each other to be heard, and I'm standing right in the middle of it. 

I'll try to focus on one thing, just one normal thing, like my electric bill—the one with the red final notice print on the envelope that I left on my kitchen counter—but before I can even process the thought about the bill, my brain has already jumped straight to the jail. The cold concrete and the bars, just like I was telling you before. And then, before I can even blink or take a breath, I'm suddenly at the mosque, thinking about the prayers, and then instantly I'm thinking about my cleaning chemicals. You know, the heavy-duty industrial floor stripper I have to mix in the mop bucket, the one that smells like strong ammonia and burns the back of your throat if you don't ventilate the hallway right. 

It just jumps, jumps, jumps. From the bills to the jail to the mosque to the cleaning chemicals, all in a split second, before I can even catch one single thought to hold onto it. It's like trying to catch a specific raindrop in a hurricane. So when I'm talking, when all those words come tumbling out of my mouth sideways, I'm just... I'm just desperately trying to keep up with the crowd up there. I'm running after my own brain, trying to get it all out before the next wave of thoughts runs me over entirely. It's exhausting, doctor, it really is, just trying to catch a single thought in all that rushing.
Do you have times when your thoughts are clear and organized, and if so, how often do those times occur?

Clear and organized? Doctor, I... I feel like we might be going around in circles a bit here, because like I've been trying to say since I first walked into this room, those clear times just don't happen for me anymore. Not for a very, very long time. If I had times where everything was clear and organized, I'd be at work right now, buffing the linoleum floors on the third level or emptying the recycling bins, not sitting in this clinic. 

But that is exactly what brings me here—my talking gets all mixed up, all the time. There really is no "how often do the clear times occur" because it's just a constant, everyday scramble. I try to explain about the keys, you know, just a simple everyday thing about my heavy brass work keys, and then before I know it I'm talking about the jail, and then the prayer rug, and then the chess pieces! It just keeps doing that, over and over, every single day. And the people around me, the supervisors or whoever is standing there, they just stare at me and they tell me they cannot follow what I am saying. They literally say those words to me. 

So, no, I don't get those clear times you're asking about. It's just that same tangled mess, day in and day out, spilling out everywhere until everyone is looking at me like they don't even know who I am. I really, really wish I could tell you that on Tuesdays and Thursdays my head is perfectly quiet and my sentences come out straight, but that's just not the truth of it. It's always the scramble.
Do you have any periods where your thoughts are not racing and tangled, even if it's just for a short while?

Well... well, I suppose, if you really break it down, there have been weeks... yes, there have been some weeks where the rushing isn't quite as loud. Where I'm not feeling so incredibly high up that I'm flying out of my skin, and I'm not so deeply depressed that I can't drag myself out of bed to put on my uniform. There are these calmer weeks, sure. Maybe the thoughts aren't crashing quite as fast. 

But... but even then, doctor, even when I'm not racing like a freight train or dragging like a stone, even when I've had two whole weeks of feeling somewhat level... the other things don't stop. They just don't. Even during those two weeks, I still heard him. The man in the vents. I'd be working late, maybe buffing the floors in the east corridor where it's always so quiet, and I'd hear him up there in the ductwork, just whispering and moving around in the metal. And it wasn't just him, either. Even when my mood was calm, I still knew... I still absolutely believed, without a shadow of a doubt, that the people in the building were signaling about me. 

I'd see them doing it. The office workers, the security guards, they'd tap their badges against the turnstiles a certain way, or they'd leave their coffee cups on the edge of the reception desk facing exactly towards the elevator bank. It was all a code. They were passing messages about me, warning each other when I was coming with my mop cart. So yes, maybe the racing thoughts take a break, maybe the mood levels out for a couple of weeks here and there, but the man in the vents and the signals... they never leave me alone. Even when I'm calm, they're right there. I can't escape them, doctor, I just can't.
Do you have any periods where your thoughts are completely clear and organized for an extended time?

Clear and organized for an extended time? No, no, I... I don't think you're hearing me, doctor. I really don't. Like I said, maybe I get a week or two where I'm not totally flying, but an extended time? No. Most of the time... almost all of the time since this whole nightmare started, I am just so keyed up. I am running, running, running. 

It's these stretches where I just... I can't stop talking, for one. I talk way too much, to the security guards, to the people waiting for the elevators, to anyone who will stand still for five seconds. And the plans... oh, the cleaning plans I come up with. I'll get it in my head that I need to strip and wax every single floor in the entire east wing in one night. Which is impossible, doctor, it takes a crew of three men at least two nights to do that properly, but I get so driven, so pushed from the inside, that I think I can do it all myself. I'll haul out the heavy machinery, the big floor buffers, the buckets, the gallons of stripper, and I'll just start tearing into it. I feel like I absolutely cannot slow down. My motor is just running way too hot, way too fast, and it stays like that for weeks and weeks. So no, extended clear time? That's just... that's just not my reality anymore. It's mostly just this... this endless, driven pushing.
Do you feel like you have control over your thoughts, or do they seem to have a life of their own?

Control? Doctor, control is a word that belongs to someone else's life, not mine. Not anymore. I try to hold on, I really do, but my thoughts... they absolutely have a life of their own. They don't just have a life of their own, they have a whole city of their own in there! 

It's like... it's like my brain is an engine that's had the governor taken off, and someone just put a brick on the gas pedal. The thoughts run so fast, just incredibly fast.
